newsitem.title: CANADA: Saudi suspect in Canada denied refugee hearing.
newsitem.headline: Saudi suspect in Canada denied refugee hearing.

text.p: A Saudi suspect in the 1996 truck bombing that killed 19 U.S. servicemen in Saudi Arabia will be deported from Canada, an immigration spokeswoman said on Wednesday.

The suspect, Hani Abdel-Rahim Hussein al-Sayegh, was officially informed that a conditional deportation order against him issued on May 14 was now effective, Citizenship and Immigration spokeswoman Joanne John said.

"He was informed that there will be no claim heard on his refugee status, that the minister has decided that it's not in the public interest to hear his refugee claim, and that decision by the minister makes the conditional deportation order effective," John said.

She was unable to say where Sayegh would be sent -- the leading candidates are the United States and Saudi Arabia -- and added that there was now a routine seven-day period under which the order was stayed before he could be removed.
U.S. officials have long sought to question Sayegh about the attack a year ago on the compound that housed U.S. military personnel in Dhahran in eastern Saudi Arabia.

Another Saudi who had been held in Canada on terrorism allegations, Fahad al-Shehri, has ended up in a Saudi jail despite Saudi assurances they were not interested in him, a human rights worker who worked with Shehri said.
Canada deported Shehri on May 29 and he was arrested when he arrived in Riyadh on May 30, the human rights activist, Adonis Derbas, told Reuters.
He said he had learned of Shehri's fate from talking to his family and friends.
Saudi Deputy Interior Minister Prince Ahmed bin Abdul-Aziz told the Saudi-owned newspaper Asharq al-Awsat in March that Shehri was not wanted.
"We know the man, all his family is in Saudi Arabia and he is not wanted, neither in the Khobar bombing nor in any other case. We have not been informed of any charges against him," the prince said.
"We will not ask for him to return ... He is a Saudi citizen, his country is open for him whenever he wants to return to his own country and family."
Derbas said Shehri was imprisoned since "he had the guts to apply for refugee status. They want to question him and find out what's going on."

It was Sayegh, however, who was a bigger fish for the intelligence community. The Canadian government named him as a driver in the bombing and a member of the radical Islamic group Hizbollah (Party of God).
A key question regarding his possible deportation to the United States is whether he would agree to cooperate in fingering others in the bombing.
